corrections.source_says: Use individual: participants received one of two stimulus combinations (A+D or B+C). Retain structure=within and randomized=not_stated. The paper describes balancing the numbers receiving each combination, but does not describe assigning, counterbalancing, or randomizing condition order.
corrections.quote: Next, a combination of stimuli (Stimuli A+D or Stimuli B+C) was chosen as the experimental material, and it was ensured that a similar number of participants received each combination.

confirmed: Source.version is supported: published ICED23 conference paper by Da Wang and Ji Han, Bordeaux, 24-28 July 2023, DOI 10.1017/pds.2023.181, published online by Cambridge University Press. The local PDF has 10 pages, printed pp. 1805-1814 (PDF p. 1, title/citation and publisher footer; PDF p. 10, final page).

Read all 332 lines of the markdown and all 10 PDF pages, including references. The document contains no appendix and does not state that supplementary material exists; source.supplement.exists=not_stated is appropriate (PDF pp. 1-10; references begin on PDF p. 8).

There is one within-person comparison of two stimulus types. Each participant received A+D or B+C and performed two design tasks; random allocation and condition-order randomization are not stated. No additional randomized study is reported, so no randomized people study with creativity or diversity scored on output is established (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2-3.4; PDF pp. 6-8, results through conclusion).

The analyzed sample is 20 people, below 50; these are the same participants in both stimulus conditions, not separate samples to add together. The abstract explicitly reports analysis of participant data (n=20), and Table 2 reports their preferences. A randomized count, exclusions, and exact counts receiving each stimulus combination are not reported; n_randomized=null is appropriate (PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 5, Section 3.2; PDF p. 6, Section 3.4 and Table 2).

Participant characteristics match: ages 21-30, 5 male and 15 female, 9 undergraduates and 11 postgraduates; backgrounds product/industrial 11, UI/UX 6, graphic 2, jewellery 1. Participants worked in their daily work environments using remote chat software (PDF p. 5, Section 3.2 and Table 1, checked with PDF table extraction).

The tasks combine bike with horse and headphone with stone arch, with a hand sketch required for each and a 10-minute limit per design. Ordinary images came from Google Images, and the alternative stimuli were researcher-generated fusions of the two concepts (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3.1 and Figure 1; PDF p. 6, Section 3.4).

The GAN training datasets contain 2500 bike images and 2300 headphone images. Although the prose names StyleGAN, the embedded Figure 3 explicitly labels the generator Trained StyleGAN2 Generator, supporting the form's more specific model name. Projection and movement between latent vectors, rather than textual prompting, are described (PDF p. 3, Section 2.2; PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; PDF p. 5, Figure 3, visually inspected in memory).

All three outcomes are designers' self-reported choices of which stimulus helped more. Section 3.3 states that evaluation comes from the designers themselves; Section 3.4 describes choosing the better stimulus after the tasks. The paper reports no rater-based or computed creativity/diversity scores on the sketches, supporting scored_on_output=false and criterion_3=not_met (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 3.3-3.4).
S1-O1 reported string matches exactly: novelty preferences, Generative Stimuli 11 (55%) and Image Stimuli 9 (45%), among 20 participants (PDF p. 6, Table 2, checked with PDF table extraction).
S1-O2 reported string matches exactly: smoothness preferences, Generative Stimuli 16 (80%) and Image Stimuli 4 (20%), among 20 participants (PDF p. 6, Table 2, checked with PDF table extraction).
S1-O3 reported string matches exactly: usefulness preferences, Generative Stimuli 12 (60%) and Image Stimuli 8 (40%), among 20 participants (PDF p. 6, Table 2, checked with PDF table extraction).

The one_line_finding accurately reproduces Table 2 and identifies these as self-reported preferences, rather than scored sketch performance. The exclusion from the core dataset and context_class=none are supported by the below-50 sample and self-report-only outcomes; quasi_people appropriately keeps this comparison outside the documented-randomized design classes (PDF pp. 5-6, Sections 3.2-3.4 and Table 2; codebook Sections 3-4).

This is an empirical study, not a synthesis; there are no pooled estimates, confidence intervals, or standardized effects to extract. Table 3 further cross-tabulates the same participants' preferences by education, rather than reporting another study (PDF pp. 6-8, Sections 4-6 and Tables 2-3).
summary: All reported preference counts and percentages match Table 2, and exclusion remains supported by 20 participants, unstated randomization, and self-report-only outcomes. The sole correction is to record individual stimulus-combination allocation as the assignment unit, since condition-order assignment is not reported.
